sections.title: Start here: how this course works
sections.summary: What you will build, how long it takes, how every lesson works, and the assumptions behind the course.
sections.content:
## What this course is

A free, practical course for starting a small, profitable business in Kerala with almost no money. It follows the methods taught by Y Combinator's Startup School, Steve Blank's customer development and the Lean Startup: talk to customers, test cheaply, sell before you build, and let evidence decide. Every lesson ends with a real task in your area or online, so by the end you will have done the work, not just read about it.

It is written for a beginner near Kuttiady in Kozhikode district who is preparing for Kerala PSC exams, has an Android phone, an old laptop and no business budget, and wants to use AI tools. It works just as well for anyone in a similar situation.

## By the end you will have

- A tested idea, backed by at least 10 customer conversations and real pre-orders or payments
- A launched micro-business with paying customers (the target is 10)
- Your founder toolkit, built one module at a time:

| Toolkit item | Built in |
| --- | --- |
| Chosen idea with a test hypothesis | Module 2 |
| Validation evidence: interviews, experiments, pre-sales | Modules 3–4 |
| Offer: value proposition, unit economics, price list | Module 5 |
| Brand and marketing kit | Module 6 |
| Sales scripts, objection playbook and pipeline | Module 7 |
| Finance sheet: cash book, P&L, break-even, cash forecast | Module 8 |
| Compliance checklist and legal pack | Module 9 |
| Operations manual (SOPs) and AI playbook | Modules 10–11 |
| KPI dashboard and growth plan | Module 12 |
| Founder operating rules | Module 13 |
| Launch plan, launch report, one-page business plan and pitch | Module 14 |

## How long it takes

| Pace | Calendar time | Hours a week | Total work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Part-time (the default) | Week 0, then 32 weeks: about 7.5 months | About 6 | About 47 hours |
| Full-time | About 8 weeks | About 24 | About 47 hours |

Pick your pace and start date on the course page. The app then shows which week you are in and what is due. The hours are honest estimates; talking to customers often takes longer than you expect, so leave some slack.

## How each lesson works

Every lesson has the same parts, in this order:

1. **ID, title, outcome and time** at the top of the page
2. **Core lesson:** one framework, explained simply
3. **Local example:** the framework applied to a Kerala business, with rupee numbers
4. **Free resources:** exactly what to study, how long it takes and when the link was checked
5. **Action task:** real work in your area or online, and the **proof to record**
6. **Template:** a copy-ready script, sheet or checklist
7. **Common mistakes** and how to avoid them
8. **Quiz:** 4 or 5 questions, with the answers at the very bottom
9. **Progress checklist:** the ticks under **Your tasks**

Each module starts with an overview page: outcomes, total time, the module project, a self-assessment rubric and a "short on time?" minimum version.

## How to use the app for this course

- Tick each task under **Your tasks** when it is done. Ticks are saved on this phone, so save a backup now and then from **Backup and courses**.
- Paste the link to your proof (a Google Drive file, sheet or photo) into the task's note.
- **This week**, on the course page, lists what is due, plus one capstone milestone at a time.
- Exam coming? Switch to exam mode (about 1 hour a week; see ENT-M01-L03) and move your start date later so the schedule matches. Your ticks are kept.

## Module map

| Module | Part-time weeks | What you do | Output for your toolkit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Founder foundations | 1–2 | Learn what founders really do, choose a path, set money and time limits | Founder Fit Sheet |
| 2. Problems and ideas | 3–4 | Collect 20 real problems, turn them into ideas, score and choose one | Idea shortlist and test hypothesis |
| 3. Customer discovery | 5–7 | Interview at least 10 people who have the problem | Customer discovery report, persona, job statements |
| 4. Validation and MVP |  | Map the business, run smoke tests and pre-sales, deliver a no-code MVP | Validation evidence pack and go / pivot / stop decision |
| 5. Business models and pricing |  | Pick a revenue model, work out profit per sale, set prices | Offer sheet: value proposition, unit economics, price list |
| 6. Marketing |  | Position and brand the business, post useful content, get found locally | Marketing kit and live profiles |
| 7. Sales |  | Build a pipeline, use scripts, handle objections, close | Sales kit and your first paying customers |
| 8. Money and finance |  | Keep books, forecast cash, find break-even, learn tax basics and funding | Finance sheet |
| 9. Legal and compliance |  | Choose a structure, register what you need, use simple agreements | Compliance checklist and legal pack |
| 10. Operations and systems |  | Write SOPs, run stock, delivery and customer service, automate | Operations manual v1 |
| 11. AI for entrepreneurs |  | Use free AI tools for research, content, support and operations, safely | AI playbook |
| 12. Growth and scaling |  | Keep customers, track KPIs, delegate and decide when to scale | KPI dashboard and growth plan |
| 13. Resilience and ethics |  | Make good decisions, handle failure, avoid burnout and scams | Founder operating rules |
| 14. Capstone: launch |  | Plan and run your launch, win paying customers, write your plan and pitch | Launch report, one-page business plan, pitch |

## Key assumptions

These decisions were made for you when the course was written. Change them if your situation is different.

1. You start part-time, about 6 hours a week next to PSC study. The full-time pace does the same work in about 8 weeks.
2. Learning costs ₹0. The business budget is your own risk limit, set in ENT-M01-L03; most learners need ₹2,000–₹10,000 for the first three months.
3. You work mainly on an Android phone and use the laptop for spreadsheets and longer writing.
4. Your business path is not decided yet. Module 1 helps you choose between freelancing → agency, a local business, digital products and online services.
5. The people and businesses in the examples (Arun, Nisha, Fathima, Meera and others) are made up. Their numbers are illustrative, so always check real local prices.
6. Laws, schemes, fees and limits were checked on 24 October 2026, and they change often. Anything marked **check current rules** links to the official source; check it before you act.
7. Nothing here is legal, tax or financial advice. Use a chartered accountant, tax practitioner or lawyer for filings, contracts and loans.
8. Every resource is free. A few need a free sign-up (Udacity, HubSpot, LEANSpark, NCFE).
9. Explanations are in simple English. Key scripts and the glossary include Malayalam.

## Honest odds

Most new businesses don't last. In the best long-run data available, from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, about half of the new business establishments that opened in 2014 had closed within five years. This course can't remove that risk, but it shrinks it: you spend little until customers pay, and you decide in advance which results mean change course or stop. ENT-M01-L01, Module 4 and Module 13 cover when not to start, when to pivot and when to stop.

## The running examples

- **Arun's ShopAssist** (freelance → agency): sets up WhatsApp Business and Google Business Profiles for shops in Kuttiady and Vatakara.
- **Nisha's Oven** (local business): home-made cakes and snacks in Kuttiady, ordered on WhatsApp.
- **Fathima's PSC Sprint** (digital product): original Kerala PSC practice packs and weekly mock tests.
- **Meera's CV Makeover** (online service): a fixed-price CV and LinkedIn rewrite for nurses and engineers applying for Gulf jobs.

## Part-time: about 6 hours a week

One course week is one calendar week. This is the default pace on the course page.

| Week | What you do | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Week 0: set up your free founder toolkit | 3 |
| 1 | ENT-M01-L01: The founder's job, honest odds and when not to start; ENT-M01-L02: Choose your business path | 6 |
| 2 | ENT-M01-L03: Your personal runway and time plan; Module 1 project and rubric | 6 |
| 3 | ENT-M02-L01: Find real problems worth solving; ENT-M02-L02: Local and online opportunities | 6 |
| 4 | ENT-M02-L03: Score your ideas and choose one to test; Module 2 project and rubric; Milestone 1 due | 6 |
| 5 | ENT-M03-L01: Plan and book customer interviews | 6 |
| 6 | ENT-M03-L02: Ask unbiased questions and take good notes | 6 |
| 7 | ENT-M03-L03: Personas and jobs to be done; Module 3 project and rubric; Milestone 2 due | 6 |

## Full-time: about 24 hours a week

Four course weeks every calendar week. Choose **Full-time** on the course page and the app counts the weeks for you. Talking to customers and waiting for replies take calendar time, so keep at least half of each day for real-world work: interviews, sales visits, deliveries.

| Calendar week | Course weeks | Focus | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0–3 | Week 0 setup; Module 1: Founder foundations; Module 2: Problems and ideas | 21 |
| 2 | 4–7 | Module 2: Problems and ideas; Module 3: Customer discovery | 24 |
| 3 | 8–11 |  | 0 |
| 4 | 12–15 |  | 0 |
| 5 | 16–19 |  | 0 |
| 6 | 20–23 |  | 0 |
| 7 | 24–27 |  | 0 |
| 8 | 28–31 |  | 0 |
| 9 | 32–32 | final checklist | 0 |

The ninth calendar week only holds the last course week, so the full-time pace takes about 8 weeks.

## A daily rhythm that fits around PSC study

- **Weekdays:** 45 minutes after your PSC study block, not before it, so the exam keeps your best hours.
- **Saturday:** 1 hour to plan the week and prepare content.
- **Sunday:** 2 hours with customers: interviews, sales visits, deliveries.
- **Sunday evening:** a 15-minute review. What did I do? What did I learn? What is next?

## When you fall behind

- **This week** shows earlier open tasks as overdue. Do the action tasks first; readings can wait.
- More than two weeks behind? Set a new start date on the course page so the weeks match your real progress. Your ticks are kept.
- Use each module's "short on time?" version when you need it.
- In the 4 weeks before a PSC exam, switch to exam mode: reply to customers and keep records, nothing new.

sections.title: Week 0: set up your free founder toolkit
sections.summary: Free tools, one Drive folder and one workbook, so every lesson has a place to save its work.
sections.content:
Week 0 takes about 3 hours. You set up free tools once, so every lesson after this has a place to save its work. Everything works on an Android phone; the laptop helps with spreadsheets.

## 1. A Founder Toolkit folder in Google Drive

Make a folder called **Founder Toolkit** with these subfolders: 01 Founder, 02 Ideas, 03 Interviews, 04 Validation, 05 Offer, 06 Marketing, 07 Sales, 08 Money, 09 Legal, 10 Operations, 11 AI, 12 Growth, 13 Founder rules, 14 Launch. Every lesson's proof goes into one of them. When a task asks for proof, copy the file's link and paste it into that task's note in this app.

## 2. The Founder Workbook

Make one Google Sheets file called **Founder Workbook**, with eight tabs: Ideas, Interviews, Experiments, Customers, Cashbook, Unit economics, KPIs and Compliance. Put each tab's header row (below) in row 1. Lessons give you the same rows again when you need them.

- **On the laptop:** copy a header line, paste it into cell A1, then choose Data → Split text to columns.
- **On the phone:** type the headings into row 1, or do this step once on the laptop.

```csv
Ideas:
No,Date,Who has it,Problem statement,How often,Pain (1-5),Current workaround,Do they pay now? (amount),Source

Interviews:
Code,Date,Who (role and place),Had the problem in the last month? (Y/N),How often,Last-time story (facts),What they did,What it cost (time or money),Pays for a workaround now? (amount),Best quote,Commitment offered,Tags,My own thoughts

Experiments:
Date,Experiment,Assumption tested,Success criterion,People reached,Replies,Sign-ups,Payments,Result,Decision

Customers:
Code,Name,Phone (with consent),Source,Stage,Last contact,Next step,Next date,Offer,Value (Rs),Paid (Rs),Notes

Cashbook:
Date,Description,Category,Money in (Rs),Money out (Rs),Mode (UPI/cash/bank),Receipt link,Balance

Unit economics:
Item,Amount per unit (Rs),Notes

KPIs:
Week,Orders or sales,Revenue (Rs),Contribution (Rs),New customers,Repeat customers,Conversations,Conversion %,Cash in bank (Rs),Notes

Compliance:
Item,Needed? (Y/N),How to get it,Cost,Official link,Status,Renewal date
```

## 3. WhatsApp Business

[WhatsApp Business](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.whatsapp.w4b) is free to download and gives you a business profile, a product catalogue, quick replies, labels and away messages. A separate number for the business is best; a second SIM and its recharges are a running cost, so count them in your risk limit. If you move your personal number to WhatsApp Business, back up your chats first and follow the steps in the app. You will set up the profile properly in ENT-M06-L01; for now, install it or decide which number you will use.

## 4. Canva (free plan)

Use Canva for posts, posters and price lists. Read the [Canva Free Media License](https://www.canva.com/policies/free-media) once: you may use its free photos and graphics in posts, ads and printed material, but not in your logo, trademark or business name.

## 5. Office tools on the old laptop

Google Sheets and Docs work in the browser. [LibreOffice (free, open-source office suite)](https://www.libreoffice.org/) works offline and is free and open source. [GnuCash (free, open-source accounting)](https://www.gnucash.org/) is optional for bookkeeping later; it runs on the laptop, not on Android. Keep the laptop light: one browser, few tabs, few extensions.

## 6. An AI assistant as your coach

The free plans of [Gemini](https://gemini.google/subscriptions/), [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/pricing) and [Claude](https://claude.com/pricing) are enough for this course (limits change; check current rules). Save this prompt and paste it at the start of a session:

```
You are my small-business coach. I live near Kuttiady,
Kozhikode, Kerala, and I am a beginner. I am taking a
practical entrepreneurship course and have about 6 hours
a week. Rules for you:
1. Ask me one question at a time.
2. Push me to talk to real customers instead of guessing.
3. Use rupee examples and Kerala context.
4. If you are not sure about a law, scheme or number,
   say so and tell me to check the official source.
5. Don't write my answers for me unless I ask.
Today I am working on: [lesson ID and task].
```

Never paste customers' names, phone numbers or private details into an AI tool. For example, Google's [Gemini API terms](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms) say that on free tiers your inputs may be used to improve Google's products and may be read by human reviewers.

## 7. Calendar and an accountability buddy

Block your weekly business slots in Google Calendar (you will fine-tune them in ENT-M01-L03). Choose an accountability buddy: a friend who is also building something, or a family member who will ask you every Sunday, "What did you do this week?"

sections.title: Capstone milestones: your real business, step by step
sections.summary: Eleven real-world milestones, from choosing an idea to a launch with paying customers. One shows in "This week" at a time.
sections.content:
The capstone is your real business. It doesn't wait until the end: it runs alongside every module, and each milestone is a real-world result, not a document. **This week** on the course page shows one milestone at a time, from the week after the previous one until its due week.

| Due by week | Milestone | Evidence | Built in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | One idea chosen, with a test hypothesis and a kill signal | Hypothesis paragraph in the Ideas tab | Module 2 |
| 7 | 10 real conversations with people who have the problem | Tagged notes for 10 or more interviews | Module 3 |
| 10 | First money or a clear answer | At least 3 pre-orders, deposits or paid trials, or a written pivot or stop decision | Module 4 |
| 12 | Your offer and price shown to at least 20 potential customers | Price test log with 20 or more people | Module 5 |
| 15 | Customers can find you | WhatsApp Business profile plus one public listing or page, with real reviews or posts | Module 6 |
| 18 | 50 sales conversations logged, with paying customers who are not friends or family | Pipeline in the Customers tab | Module 7 |
| 21 | Every rupee in and out recorded for 4 weeks | Cash book and your first monthly P&L | Module 8 |
| 23 | The registrations your business needs are done or applied for | Compliance checklist with dates and receipts | Module 9 |
| 26 | Your top 3 repeated jobs have SOPs, and one is automated or delegated | SOP documents and a time-saved note | Modules 10–11 |
| 29 | Monthly KPI review done, with at least one repeat or referred customer | KPI dashboard and review notes | Modules 12–13 |
| 32 | Launch done, with 10 paying customers in total or your own written target | Launch report, one-page plan and 90-day plan | Module 14 |

## How to use the milestones

- Tick a milestone only when the evidence exists, and paste a link to it in the milestone's note.
- Missing a milestone is information, not failure. Ask why: the wrong customer, the wrong offer, the wrong channel, or not enough attempts? Then adjust and try again before the next milestone.
- If Milestone 3 shows no real demand after two honest tests, use the go / pivot / stop decision in ENT-M04-L04 before you go further. It is cheaper to change course in week 10 than in week 30.

## Why "first money" comes so early

Pre-orders, deposits and paid trials in Module 4 are the strongest evidence that your idea works. They also mean your first revenue usually arrives around week 9 or 10, long before the formal launch in Module 14.

sections.title: Module 1: Founder foundations
sections.summary: Before you look for ideas, get clear on three things: what running a business really involves, which kind of business fits your life right now, and how much money and time you can safely put in. This module turns those into numbers and rules you will use for the rest of the course.
sections.content:
## Overview

Before you look for ideas, get clear on three things: what running a business really involves, which kind of business fits your life right now, and how much money and time you can safely put in. This module turns those into numbers and rules you will use for the rest of the course.

One idea runs through it: a business is a series of small, cheap experiments, not one big bet. You set your limits now, while you are calm, so you never risk more than you can afford to lose.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain what a founder does each week and the real odds of a new business surviving
- Choose one business path to test first, and a backup, using scores and a real conversation
- State your survival number, runway, risk limit and weekly time plan
- Decide your personal start conditions: when to start, when to pause and when not to start

## Time

About 12 hours in total: 10 hours of lessons and 2 hours for the module project. Part-time: weeks 1–2.

## Lessons

1. ENT-M01-L01: The founder's job, honest odds and when not to start (about 3 hours)
2. ENT-M01-L02: Choose your business path (about 3 hours)
3. ENT-M01-L03: Your personal runway and time plan (about 4 hours)

## Module project: Founder Fit Sheet

1. Make one Google Doc called "Founder Fit Sheet" with four parts: your start conditions (L01), your path scores and choice (L02), your runway and risk limit (L03), and your weekly time plan (L03).
2. Add your notes from the two business-owner conversations (L01) and the conversation with someone on your top path (L02).
3. At the top, write three sentences: the path you will test first, the most you will risk (rupees and hours a week), and the date you will review this choice (the end of week 10).
4. Show it to one person you trust and ask, "What am I not seeing?" Write down their answer at the bottom.

**Proof to record:** Your Founder Fit Sheet, saved in your Founder Toolkit folder, with the reviewer's comment at the bottom.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Honesty about limits | Time and money not stated | Stated, but the numbers are guesses | Real numbers from a week of tracking |
| Path choice | Picked on feeling | Scored, but no talk with anyone on that path | Scored, discussed with someone on that path, backup chosen |
| Risk limit | None | A rupee limit only | A rupee limit, an hours limit and a stop rule |
| Time plan | "Whenever I'm free" | Weekly hours, but no fixed slots | Fixed slots that protect PSC study, shared with family |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- L01: fill in "My start conditions" (20 minutes) and skip the readings.
- L02: score the four paths; move the conversation with someone on your top path to week 3.
- L03: work out your survival number and risk limit, tracking spending for 3 days instead of 7.

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Quitting PSC prep or a job "to focus" before any customer has paid.** Keep your income and your exam plan, and test on the side.
- **Copying a success story.** You only hear from the people who survived. Ask what the closed businesses had in common too.
- **Leaving limits vague.** "I'll spend a little" can turn into ₹40,000. Write a number down.

sections.title: ENT-M01-L01: The founder's job, honest odds and when not to start
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain what a founder actually does each week, state the real odds of a new business surviving, and write your own start conditions. **Time:** about 3 hours (1.5 hours study, 1.5 hours action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

**A business is simple to describe.** You solve a problem for people, they pay you more than it costs you to solve it, and they come back or tell others. Everything else is detail. Your job as a founder is to make that loop work, one customer at a time.

In a small business, a founder's week usually looks like this:

- **Finding customers:** talking to people, posting, following up. Most beginners spend far too little time here.
- **Delivering:** baking the cake, setting up the shop's WhatsApp, writing the question pack.
- **Collecting money and keeping records:** every rupee in and out, written down.
- **Improving:** asking customers what to fix, then fixing it.

"Being the boss" is not on the list. Early on, you are the salesperson, the delivery person and the accountant.

### Startup or small business?

You will hear two words. A **startup**, in the Y Combinator sense, is a company built to grow very fast, often with investors' money, and most of them fail. A **small business** (a micro-enterprise) aims to be profitable early and grow steadily: a home bakery, a design service, a tuition centre. This course aims for the second first: a business that earns real money within months. Paul Graham calls a startup that earns just enough to cover its founders' living costs "ramen profitable". That is a good first target for you too.

### The honest odds

Many new businesses close. The best long-run public data comes from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. Of new business establishments that opened in 2014, about 80% were still open after one year, about 51% after five years and about 35% after ten years. India has no equally reliable public figure, so treat this as a rough guide. Remember too that some closures are owners moving on, not failures.

Small businesses usually close for a few repeating reasons:

- **No real demand.** Not enough people wanted it enough to pay.
- **Running out of cash.** Money was spent before money came in.
- **Prices too low.** Sales came in, but each sale lost money.
- **The founder burned out or lost interest.**

Every module of this course attacks one of these.

### Think in experiments, not bets

The safest way to start is with small, cheap tests that each answer one question. Do people have this problem? Will they pay? Can I deliver it at a profit? Decide in advance how much money and time you can afford to lose, and never go past it. When a test fails, you lose a little and learn a lot.

### When not to start (yet)

Pause, or start smaller, if any of these is true:

1. You would have to borrow to start: a gold loan, a credit card balance, a private money lender, or family money without written terms.
2. You have less than three months of essential expenses saved and no other income.
3. Your PSC exam is only a few weeks away. Exam weeks come first; the business can wait.
4. The idea needs a big spend (a shop lease, machines, stock) before a single customer has paid.
5. You are in the middle of a health or family crisis.
6. Someone wants a joining fee for you to "start your own business". That is the classic sign of a pyramid scheme, not a business.

None of these means "never". They mean "not like this, and not now".

## Local example

These two people are made up, but their stories are common in Kerala towns.

**Shibu** saw busy juice shops in Kozhikode and opened one on Kuttiady's main road with a ₹4 lakh loan: ₹1.5 lakh for interiors, ₹1 lakh for machines, a ₹1 lakh rent deposit and ₹50,000 of stock. Rent was ₹15,000 a month. In the monsoon months, sales fell to about ₹800 a day, below his costs. He closed after eight months, still owing most of the loan.

**Nisha** wanted to sell home-made cakes. She first baked for two neighbours' birthdays at ₹650 each, using her own oven and about ₹2,000 of ingredients. Both ordered again and told friends. After two months she had 15 regular customers. She bought a bigger oven only when she already had ₹10,000 of advance orders for Christmas.

Same town, same years. The difference was not talent. Nisha tested demand before she spent; Shibu spent before he tested.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [YC: "Should You Start A Startup?" (Harj Taggar)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BUE-icVYRFU) | Watch the whole talk | about 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Paul Graham: "Startups in 13 Sentences"](https://paulgraham.com/13sentences.html) | Read it all; mark points 8 and 9, on spending little and ramen profitability | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Paul Graham: "Why to Not Not Start a Startup"](https://paulgraham.com/notnot.html) | Read the list of reasons people give for not starting, and note which ones apply to you | 25 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 1](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/1-introduction) | Sections 1.1 Entrepreneurship Today and 1.3 The Entrepreneurial Mindset | 40 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [US Bureau of Labor Statistics: survival of new establishments, Table 7](https://www.bls.gov/bdm/us_age_naics_00_table7.txt) | Optional: find establishments that opened in March 2014 and read their survival rate year by year | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Pick two people near you who run a small business: a shop owner, a home baker, a tailor, a tuition teacher. Choose people you can meet or call this week.
2. Ask for 15 minutes: "I'm learning how small businesses start. Can I ask you five questions? I'm not selling anything."
3. Ask the five questions in the first template below. Write their answers within an hour, while you still remember the details.
4. Fill in "My start conditions" honestly. For every "no", write what would have to change and by when. (You set your exact risk limit in ENT-M01-L03; for now, write a rough number.)
5. Save both in your Founder Toolkit folder as "M01 founder reality notes".

**Proof to record:** Notes from two conversations with business owners and your filled start-conditions checklist, saved in your Founder Toolkit folder.

## Template: founder reality interview

```
FOUNDER REALITY INTERVIEW (15 minutes)
Name, business, years running:

1. How did you get your first 5 customers?
2. How much did you spend before your first sale? On what?
3. When did the business first make a profit?
4. What was your hardest month, and what happened?
5. If you started again, what would you do differently?

One thing that surprised me:
```

## Template: my start conditions

```
MY START CONDITIONS (write yes or no)
___ I can start without borrowing money
___ I have 3 months of essential expenses saved,
    or another income that covers them
___ My next PSC exam is more than 4 weeks away
___ My first test costs less than my risk limit
___ My family knows my plan and my time limits
___ Nobody is asking me for a joining fee

For each "no":
What must change: ____________________
By when: ____________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Starting with a big spend.** Shops, machines and stock come after paying customers, not before. Test with what you already have.
- **Believing only success stories.** For every shop that made it, others closed quietly. Ask owners about their hardest month, not only their best one.
- **Treating doubts as weakness.** Writing down when not to start is a strength. It stops you from making a bad bet on an excited day.
- **Asking only family for advice.** Family often fears risk and friends want to encourage you. Talk to people who actually run businesses.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is a founder's main job in a new small business?
    - A) Managing staff
    - B) Finding customers, delivering, collecting money and improving
    - C) Designing the logo and the shop
    - D) Applying for loans
2. In US government data for establishments that opened in 2014, roughly how many were still open five years later?
    - A) About 10%
    - B) About half
    - C) About 90%
    - D) Nearly all
3. Which of these is a reason to pause or start smaller?
    - A) One customer has already paid you
    - B) You would need a gold loan to start
    - C) Your exam is four months away
    - D) Your first test costs ₹500
4. What does "ramen profitable" mean?
    - A) Selling noodles
    - B) Earning just enough to cover the founders' living costs
    - C) Making a profit in the first week
    - D) Raising money from investors
5. Someone offers you a "business opportunity" for a ₹15,000 joining fee, with earnings from recruiting others. What should you do?
    - A) Pay, because high returns are promised
    - B) Ask for a discount
    - C) Treat it as a sign of a pyramid scheme and walk away
    - D) Recruit your family first

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the resources in the table (about 1.5 hours)
- **Action:** interview two local business owners and fill in your start conditions. It is done when your proof is saved: notes from two conversations with business owners and your filled start-conditions checklist, saved in your Founder Toolkit folder.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Early on you run the core loop yourself. Staff, logos and loans come later, if at all.
2. **B.** About 51% were still open after five years (BLS Table 7). India has no equally reliable figure.
3. **B.** Borrowing to start means you can lose more than you can afford. Start with what you have.
4. **B.** Paul Graham uses it for a business that pays its founders' basic living costs, which gives you time and freedom.
5. **C.** India's Consumer Protection (Direct Selling) Rules, 2021 ban promoting pyramid and money circulation schemes. Real businesses earn from customers, not joining fees.

sections.title: ENT-M01-L02: Choose your business path
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Compare the four beginner business paths and pick one to test first, plus a backup, using scores and one real conversation. **Time:** about 3 hours (1 hour 15 minutes study, 1 hour 45 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

There are many kinds of business, but four paths suit a beginner with little money. Each one makes money differently and fits a different life.

| Path | How you earn | Rough start cost | Time to first ₹ | Can it grow? | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Freelance → agency | You sell a skill (design, setup, writing) job by job, then hire or partner to take on more work | ₹0–₹5,000 | Days to weeks | Yes, once others do part of the work | Income stops when you stop; late payments |
| Local business | You sell a product or service in your area: food, repairs, tuition | ₹2,000–₹50,000 or more | Days to weeks | Slowly: more capacity, more areas | Stock, rent, licences, spoilage |
| Digital products | You make something once (a question pack, templates, a course) and sell it many times | ₹0–₹2,000 | Weeks to months | Yes: another copy costs almost nothing | Needs an audience; easy to copy |
| Online services | You sell one fixed package online (a ₹999 CV rewrite, online classes) to many customers | ₹0–₹3,000 | Days to weeks | Yes, with templates and helpers | Competition; your time is the limit |

The start costs are rough examples for very small first versions. Check real costs for your own idea.

**Freelancing or online service?** A freelancer does custom work for each client. An online service sells the same package, at the same price, to many people. Many people start as freelancers and turn their most common job into a packaged service. An **agency** is the next step: you win the clients and others help deliver.

### What makes a path fit you

Score each path from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent):

1. **Time to first rupee:** how soon could you earn from it?
2. **Start cost:** can you start within your risk limit?
3. **Your skills:** can you deliver it now, or after a few weeks of practice?
4. **Your time:** does it fit about 6 hours a week next to PSC prep, without fixed shop hours?
5. **Your network:** do you already know people who would buy, or who know buyers?
6. **Interest:** would you still do it in a bad week?
7. **Long-term potential:** could it grow into a real income?

Your network matters more than most people think. If your uncle runs three textile shops, a service for shops has a head start. If you have helped PSC aspirants before, a PSC product does.

You are not choosing forever. Pick one path to test first and one backup. Paths combine well over time: an AI-assisted service for local shops now, and a digital product for the same shops next year.

## Local example

Here is how Arun, a made-up learner much like you (near Kuttiady, about 6 hours a week, an Android phone, an old laptop and new AI skills), scores four ideas, one per path. All four come back as running examples throughout the course: Arun builds ShopAssist, Nisha runs Nisha's Oven, Fathima makes PSC Sprint and Meera runs CV Makeover.

| Question | ShopAssist: WhatsApp and Google setup for shops | Nisha's Oven: home-made cakes | PSC Sprint: practice-question packs | CV Makeover: ₹999 CV and LinkedIn for Gulf jobs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Path | Freelance → agency | Local business | Digital product | Online service |
| Time to first ₹ | 5 | 4 | 2 | 4 |
| Start cost | 5 | 3 | 5 | 5 |
| Skills | 4 | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| Fits 6 h a week | 3 | 2 | 4 | 4 |
| Network | 4 | 3 | 4 | 3 |
| Interest | 4 | 2 | 4 | 3 |
| Potential | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| **Total (of 35)** | **29** | **19** | **26** | **25** |

For Arun, ShopAssist is the first test and PSC Sprint the backup. Nisha, who loves baking and owns a good oven, would score the home bakery much higher. The scores belong to the person, not to the idea.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 2](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/2-introduction) | Sections 2.3 Entrepreneurial Pathways and 2.4 Frameworks to Inform Your Entrepreneurial Path | 45 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Paul Graham: "Ramen Profitable"](https://paulgraham.com/ramenprofitable.html) | Read it all | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [MIT OpenCourseWare 15.390 New Enterprises (2013): video tutorials](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/15-390-new-enterprises-spring-2013/video_galleries/video-tutorials/) | Lecture 4: Three Ways to Start a Company (length not listed) | budget 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. For each of the four paths, write one concrete idea you could start from your town or your phone. One line each.
2. Score all four with the template below. Be strict: a 5 means "I could do this next week".
3. Ask one person who knows you well to score only the "skills" and "network" rows for you, before they see your scores. Compare the two.
4. Find one person already on your top path (a freelancer, a home baker, someone selling a digital product) and ask: "What do you wish you had known in your first month?" Write down the answer.
5. Write your choice: first path, backup path, and one sentence on why.

**Proof to record:** Your scored path table (including the second person's scores) and your notes from the conversation with someone on your top path.

## Template: path scores (paste into Google Sheets)

```csv
Question,Freelance to agency,Local business,Digital product,Online service
My idea (one line),,,,
Time to first rupee (1-5),,,,
Start cost (1-5),,,,
My skills (1-5),,,,
Fits my time (1-5),,,,
My network (1-5),,,,
My interest (1-5),,,,
Long-term potential (1-5),,,,
Total,=SUM(B3:B9),=SUM(C3:C9),=SUM(D3:D9),=SUM(E3:E9)
```

## Template: my path choice

```
First path to test: ____________
Backup path: ____________
Why (one sentence): ____________
Person I asked on this path: ____________
What they wish they had known: ____________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Choosing the most fashionable path.** Dropshipping, trading and "passive income" videos make things look easy. Score them like any other path; most score low on start cost or risk.
- **Ignoring your network.** People you already know are your fastest first customers. A path that uses them can save you months.
- **Starting with a digital product and no audience.** Digital products sell to people who already trust you. With no audience yet, a service usually earns sooner and builds that trust.
- **Treating the choice as permanent.** You are choosing what to test first. You will review this choice at the end of Module 4 with real evidence.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What is the main difference between freelancing and an online service?
    - A) Freelancing is always offline
    - B) An online service sells one fixed package to many customers; freelancing is custom work for each client
    - C) An online service needs a registered company
    - D) There is no difference
2. Which path usually costs least to sell one more unit?
    - A) Local business
    - B) Freelancing
    - C) Digital products
    - D) Online services
3. Why does the "network" score matter?
    - A) Banks check it
    - B) People you know can buy or introduce buyers, which shortens the time to your first rupee
    - C) It decides your tax rate
    - D) It doesn't matter
4. Your scores are freelance → agency 29 and digital product 26. What should you do?
    - A) Start both, full-time
    - B) Test freelancing first and keep the digital product as a backup
    - C) Pick the digital product because it scales
    - D) Wait until one path scores 35

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax 2.3 and 2.4, "Ramen Profitable" and the MIT lecture (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
- **Action:** score the four paths, get a second opinion and talk to someone on your top path. It is done when your proof is saved: your scored path table (including the second person's scores) and your notes from the conversation with someone on your top path.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Packaging the work (same scope, same price) is what turns freelancing into a service that can grow.
2. **C.** Once a digital product is made, another copy costs almost nothing. The hard part is finding buyers.
3. **B.** Your first customers almost always come from people you know or people they know.
4. **B.** Test one path at a time. The backup is ready if the first test fails.

sections.title: ENT-M01-L03: Your personal runway and time plan
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Know your monthly survival number, your runway in months, the most money and time you will risk, and the weekly hours you can protect next to PSC prep. **Time:** about 4 hours (30 minutes study (plus an optional hour), 3.5 hours action spread over the week).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Money and time are your two limits. Writing them down now stops you from spending too much on an excited day, or quitting on a tired one.

### Your survival number and runway

Your **survival number** is what you need each month for essentials: your share of household costs, food, phone, travel, loan payments (EMIs), insurance and study materials. It is not what you would like to spend. It is what you can't avoid.

Your **runway** is how many months you could manage if your income stopped:

**Runway (months) = savings you can use ÷ (survival number − other monthly income)**

If your other income already covers your survival number, your runway has no limit. That is the best position to start a business from, because you can test ideas without needing them to pay the bills.

### Keep three pots of money

1. **Emergency money:** ideally 3 months of your survival number. Never use it for the business.
2. **Living money:** your normal monthly spending.
3. **Risk money:** the most you will spend on the business before it pays you back. This is your **risk limit**.

Choose a risk limit you could lose completely without hurting your family or your exam plan. Because this course tests before it spends, ₹2,000 to ₹10,000 for the first three months is enough for most learners. Add a time limit too, for example "6 hours a week, and only 1 hour a week in the 4 weeks before an exam".

### Money you should never use to start

- Gold loans, or pledging family gold
- A credit card balance you can't clear in full that month
- Private money lenders who charge daily or weekly interest (often called "blade" lenders in Kerala)
- Loan apps you can't confirm are linked to an RBI-regulated lender
- Family money without a written note of the amount, how it will be repaid and what happens if the business fails

### Your time plan

Six hours a week is enough to start a small business if the hours are fixed. Here is one plan that works next to PSC study:

| Day | Time | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday to Thursday | 45 minutes after PSC study | Lessons, messages, records |
| Saturday | 1 hour | Planning and content |
| Sunday | 2 hours | Customer conversations, sales, delivery |

**Exam mode:** in the 4 weeks before a PSC exam, drop to about 1 hour a week. Reply to customers and keep records; start nothing new. In this app, move your start date later so the schedule matches your real pace. Your ticks are kept.

**Full-time track:** about 24 hours a week, for example 4 hours a day for 6 days, with at least half of that time spent with customers rather than at a screen.

This is general information, not financial advice. If you have debts or people who depend on you, talk your limits through with someone you trust.

## Local example

Arun, a learner near Kuttiady who appears all through this course, lists his essentials: ₹4,000 to the household, ₹1,200 for food outside, ₹1,500 for bus and petrol, ₹300 for the phone, ₹500 for PSC materials and ₹1,500 for everything else. Survival number: **₹9,000 a month**. Usable savings: ₹30,000. No other income right now.

Runway = ₹30,000 ÷ (₹9,000 − ₹0) = **about 3.3 months**.

That is short. So Arun keeps ₹27,000 as emergency money and sets a risk limit of **₹3,000 for the first three months**, plus 6 hours a week. Any spending above ₹3,000 must come out of money customers have already paid. He also looks for a small steady income, such as two evening tuition students, so the business never has to pay the household bills in its first year.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [NCFE: National Centre for Financial Education (free e-learning)](https://ncfe.org.in/) | Optional: register free and take the e-learning module on financial planning (budgets and saving) | about 1 hour | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 1](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/1-introduction) | Section 1.2 Entrepreneurial Vision and Goals | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Paul Graham: "Default Alive or Default Dead?"](https://paulgraham.com/aord.html) | Read it all, thinking of your own household as the "startup" | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Starting today, write down every rupee you spend for 7 days, in a notebook or a sheet. Include small things: tea, recharges, bus fares.
2. At the end of the 7 days, fill in the runway calculator below with your real numbers.
3. Decide your three pots. Write down your emergency amount, your risk limit in rupees and your time limit in hours a week.
4. Block your weekly business slots in Google Calendar, or write them on paper and stick it where you study.
5. Tell one family member your plan, your risk limit and your exam-mode rule. Ask them to remind you if you break it.

**Proof to record:** Your 7-day spending record, the filled runway calculator and a photo or screenshot of your weekly time plan.

## Template: runway calculator (paste into Google Sheets)

```csv
Item,Monthly amount in rupees
Household share,
Food,
Travel,
Phone and internet,
Loan EMIs,
Insurance,
Study materials,
Other essentials,
SURVIVAL NUMBER,=SUM(B2:B9)
Other monthly income,
Savings I can use,
RUNWAY in months,=B12/(B10-B11)
Emergency pot (3 months),=3*B10
Risk limit for the first 3 months,
Time limit in hours a week,
```

## Template: weekly time plan

```
MY WEEKLY TIME PLAN
Business hours a week: ___
Mon to Thu: ___ to ___ (lessons, messages, records)
Saturday: ___ to ___ (planning, content)
Sunday: ___ to ___ (customers, sales, delivery)

Next exam date: ___
Exam mode starts (4 weeks before): ___
In exam mode I only reply to customers and keep records.
Person who will remind me: ___
```

## Common mistakes

- **Guessing your expenses.** Small daily spends add up and are easy to forget. Track a full week before you calculate anything.
- **Mixing the pots.** If business money and household money share one wallet, you can't tell whether the business makes money. Keep separate records from day one.
- **Planning 20 hours a week on paper.** Plan the hours you really have. Six fixed hours beat twenty imaginary ones.
- **Having no exam-mode rule.** Decide now what you will pause before an exam, so you neither panic nor feel guilty when the time comes.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Your survival number is ₹8,000, other income is ₹3,000 a month and usable savings are ₹20,000. What is your runway?
    - A) 2.5 months
    - B) 4 months
    - C) 6.7 months
    - D) 10 months
2. Which money is fine to use for your first business test?
    - A) A gold loan
    - B) Your emergency pot
    - C) Your risk money, set in advance
    - D) A loan app you found on social media
3. What is a risk limit?
    - A) The most a bank will lend you
    - B) The most money and time you will put in before the business pays you back
    - C) Your monthly salary
    - D) The GST threshold
4. What should you do in the 4 weeks before a PSC exam?
    - A) Launch a new product
    - B) Switch to exam mode: reply to customers and keep records only
    - C) Close the business
    - D) Work double hours to get ahead
5. Why is it good to start when other income covers your survival number?
    - A) You can borrow more
    - B) You can test ideas without needing the business to pay your bills yet
    - C) You no longer need records
    - D) Your taxes are lower

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** OpenStax 1.2 and "Default Alive or Default Dead?" (30 minutes), plus NCFE if you have time
- **Action:** track 7 days of spending, calculate your runway and set your risk and time limits. It is done when your proof is saved: your 7-day spending record, the filled runway calculator and a photo or screenshot of your weekly time plan.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** ₹20,000 ÷ (₹8,000 − ₹3,000) = 4 months.
2. **C.** Risk money is the amount you decided you can lose without harm.
3. **B.** It is your own rule, set while you are calm, so excitement never decides how much you spend.
4. **B.** Exam mode keeps existing customers happy without stealing study time.
5. **B.** Without pressure to earn at once, you can run honest tests and walk away from bad ideas.

sections.title: Module 2: Problems and ideas
sections.summary: Good businesses start from real problems, not clever ideas. In this module you collect problems from your town, your own life and online groups, turn the best ones into business ideas, and score them to pick one to test.
sections.content:
## Overview

Good businesses start from real problems, not clever ideas. In this module you collect problems from your town, your own life and online groups, turn the best ones into business ideas, and score them to pick one to test.

You finish with one idea, two backups and a test hypothesis that says exactly what result would prove you wrong.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Collect 20 real problems from observation and conversations, written as clear problem statements
- Spot local, seasonal and online opportunities and estimate a market from the bottom up
- Score your ideas with a weighted scorecard and choose one to test, with a hypothesis, a kill signal and a date

## Time

About 12 hours in total: 10 hours of lessons and 2 hours for the module project. Part-time: weeks 3–4.

## Lessons

1. ENT-M02-L01: Find real problems worth solving (about 3 hours)
2. ENT-M02-L02: Local and online opportunities (about 3 hours)
3. ENT-M02-L03: Score your ideas and choose one to test (about 4 hours)

## Module project: Idea shortlist

1. In the Ideas tab: your problem log of 20 problems (L01).
2. Below it: your 10 idea statements and the size checks for your top three (L02).
3. Your weighted scorecard, with your chosen idea and two backups (L03).
4. One paragraph at the top: your test hypothesis, kill signal and date, and why you chose this idea over the backups.

**Proof to record:** The Ideas tab of your Founder Workbook with 20 problems, 10 ideas, the scorecard and your hypothesis paragraph.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Problem quality | Ideas with no problems behind them | Problems, but vague ("people need X") | Specific statements with who, how often, cost and workaround |
| Evidence | Only my own guesses | A few conversations | Observation, at least 8 conversations and online sources |
| Scoring | Not done | Done alone; my favourite won | Weighted, second opinion, kill criteria applied honestly |
| Hypothesis | None | "People will like it" | Customer, price, offer, kill signal and date |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, when PSC prep or work leaves little time:

- L01: log 10 problems instead of 20, from five conversations and Google Maps reviews.
- L02: write 5 idea statements and skip Google Trends.
- L03: score only your top 5 ideas, but still do the three quick chats.

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Falling in love with the first idea.** Log 20 problems before you let yourself choose.
- **Picking a problem nobody pays to solve today.** Look for current spending or time spent on workarounds.
- **Saying the market is "everyone".** Name one group you can reach this month.

sections.title: ENT-M02-L01: Find real problems worth solving
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Collect 20 real problems from your town, your own life and online groups, written as clear problem statements. **Time:** about 3 hours (1 hour study, 2 hours action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Most beginners start with a solution ("I'll make an app for…") and then look for people who need it. It works much better the other way round. Find a problem people already have, already spend time or money on, and would be glad to see solved. Then build the business around it.

### Where problems hide

- **Your own life.** What annoys you every week? Paul Graham's advice is to look first at problems you have yourself, because you already understand them.
- **People around you.** Shop owners, farmers, students, parents, elders, families with someone working in the Gulf. Ask what wastes their time or money.
- **Complaints.** One-star and two-star Google Maps reviews of local businesses are a list of unmet needs. So are the complaints that repeat in WhatsApp and Facebook groups.
- **Queues and workarounds.** A queue, a handwritten notice, a relative who "helps out every evening": each one is a problem being solved badly.
- **Boring jobs.** Paul Graham calls it schlep blindness: people overlook problems because the work looks dull, like paperwork, follow-ups or online applications. Dull problems often pay well, because few people want to solve them.

### What makes a problem worth solving

| Test | Good sign | Bad sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frequency | Happens every week or every season | Once in a lifetime |
| Pain | Costs money, sales, time or sleep | "It would be nice" |
| Current spending | People already pay, or spend hours on a workaround | Nobody does anything about it |
| Reach | You can talk to 20 of these people this month | You don't know any of them |
| Growth | More people will have it next year | It is disappearing |

### Write it as a problem statement

Use this shape: **[Who] struggles to [do what] because [why]. It costs them [time, money or stress]. Today they [workaround].**

For example: "Textile shop owners in Kuttiady struggle to reply to WhatsApp enquiries in the evening rush because they are at the counter. They lose sales to shops that reply faster. Today a family member replies late at night."

To dig deeper, ask "why?" up to five times. "Why do you reply late?" "Because I'm billing." "Why can't someone else reply?" "Because only I know the prices." Now you have found the real problem: the prices live only in the owner's head.

## Local example

In one week, Arun logged problems like these (the people are made up; the patterns are common):

1. Textile and mobile shops get dozens of WhatsApp enquiries in the evening and reply hours later, after customers have bought elsewhere. (Heard from three shop owners.)
2. Parents want home-made birthday cakes without artificial colours, but the nearest home baker they trust is in Vatakara. (Two mothers at a school gate.)
3. PSC aspirants in nearby villages can't afford ₹1,000 or more for coaching-centre mock tests, and the free tests they find online don't follow the latest pattern. (Four aspirants in a study group.)
4. Nurses applying abroad send CVs in old formats and rarely hear back. (A cousin in Dubai and two nursing students.)
5. Elderly parents of Gulf workers struggle with online bill payments and pension updates. (Overheard in an Akshaya centre queue.)

Each of these became an idea later in this module. None of them started as an idea.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Paul Graham: "How to Get Startup Ideas"](https://paulgraham.com/startupideas.html) | Read the first half, up to and including the part on noticing problems | 30 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Paul Graham: "Schlep Blindness"](https://paulgraham.com/schlep.html) | Read it all | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 6](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/6-introduction) | Section 6.1 Problem Solving to Find Entrepreneurial Solutions | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. **Observation walk (45 minutes).** Walk through your town's main road, market or bus stand. Note every queue, complaint, handwritten notice and workaround you see.
2. **Five quick conversations (45 minutes).** Ask five different people: "What was the most annoying thing about [shopping, your shop, studying, your phone] this month?" Then ask: "What did you do about it?" Don't mention any idea.
3. **Review mining (20 minutes).** On Google Maps, open five businesses in your area and read their one-star and two-star reviews. Write down the problem behind each complaint.
4. **Online groups (10 minutes).** Scan two groups you belong to (WhatsApp, Facebook, a subreddit) for complaints and questions that repeat.
5. Log 20 problems in the Ideas tab of your Founder Workbook as problem statements. Mark each with how often it happens, how painful it is and whether people pay for a workaround today.

**Proof to record:** Your problem log with at least 20 problems, each with its source.

## Template: problem log (paste into the Ideas tab)

```csv
No,Date,Who has it,Problem statement,How often,Pain (1-5),Current workaround,Do they pay now? (amount),Source
1,,,,,,,,
2,,,,,,,,
3,,,,,,,,
```

## Common mistakes

- **Starting with a solution.** "An app for farmers" is not a problem. Ask what the farmer struggled with this month.
- **Asking "Would you use…?"** People say yes to be polite. Ask what they did the last time the problem happened.
- **Logging only your own problems.** Your life is one data point. Aim for at least 15 of the 20 problems to come from other people.
- **Skipping boring problems.** Paperwork, follow-ups and record-keeping are often the problems people pay most to escape.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which of these is a problem statement rather than a solution?
    - A) An app for tuition centres
    - B) Tuition centre owners in Perambra struggle to collect fees on time because parents forget; they spend about 5 hours a month making calls
    - C) A WhatsApp bot for parents
    - D) A website for students
2. Which sign best shows that a problem is worth solving?
    - A) People say it is a great idea
    - B) People already spend money or hours on a workaround
    - C) It is trending on Instagram
    - D) Your friend likes it
3. What does Paul Graham mean by "schlep blindness"?
    - A) Avoiding hard physical work
    - B) Overlooking good problems because solving them looks tedious
    - C) Ignoring your competitors
    - D) Being afraid of risk
4. Why read one-star reviews of local businesses?
    - A) To copy those businesses
    - B) They reveal unmet needs that customers care about
    - C) To reply to them
    - D) To improve your own search ranking

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the first half of "How to Get Startup Ideas", "Schlep Blindness" and OpenStax 6.1 (about 1 hour)
- **Action:** do an observation walk, five conversations and review mining, then log 20 problems. It is done when your proof is saved: your problem log with at least 20 problems, each with its source.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** It names who has the problem, why it happens and what it costs. The others are solutions.
2. **B.** Spending, in money or time, is evidence. Compliments are not.
3. **B.** Tedious problems are often left unsolved, which makes them good opportunities.
4. **B.** Each complaint points to something customers wanted and didn't get.

sections.title: ENT-M02-L02: Local and online opportunities
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Map opportunities in your area and online, turn your best problems into 10 idea statements and roughly size the market for your top three. **Time:** about 3 hours (1 hour 15 minutes study, 1 hour 45 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

A problem becomes an opportunity when enough people have it, you can reach them, and they can pay. This lesson shows you where to look and how to do a quick size check.

### Where opportunities show up around Kuttiady

- **What people leave town for.** If people travel to Vatakara, Perambra or Kozhikode for something (a cake, a repair, a document service, coaching), there may be room for it nearer home.
- **Seasons and festivals.** Onam, Vishu, Christmas, Ramadan and Eid, the wedding season, school reopening in June and the monsoon all change what people buy. Some businesses earn most of their year in a few weeks, so plan for both the peak and the slack.
- **Gulf families.** Many households have someone working abroad. The family back home often needs help with what that person used to do: payments, paperwork, repairs, shopping for elderly parents.
- **Tourism.** Places near Kuttiady such as Peruvannamuzhi, Janakikkad and Kakkayam draw visitors, who need stays, food, guides and transport.
- **Farm produce.** Coconut, arecanut, pepper and banana can become value-added products. Check food-safety and licence rules before you sell any food.
- **Local schemes.** Kerala's One Local Body One Product (OLOP) scheme asks each local body to pick and promote a local product, which can point you to products your panchayat wants to back.

### Online opportunities

- **Services for people anywhere:** CV writing, design, video editing, Malayalam–English translation, setting up online tools for small businesses.
- **Digital products for Malayali learners:** PSC practice, spoken English, exam notes, templates.
- **Local products for Malayalis elsewhere:** selling to other cities or abroad brings shipping, GST and food-safety rules, so check them first.

### Check demand quickly

**Google Trends** shows whether searches for a topic are growing, falling or seasonal. Set the region to Kerala and compare terms such as "home made cake" and "birthday cake". It shows relative interest, not exact numbers, so use it to compare, not to count.

**A bottom-up market size** is a rough count you build yourself:

**Market per year = customers you can reach × purchases per customer per year × price**

Always start from customers you could actually reach this year, never from "everyone in Kerala".

### Look at the alternatives

List at least five things your customer could do instead of buying from you, including "do nothing" and "do it myself". Your real competition is often a habit, not another business.

### The idea statement

**For [customer] who [problem], [offer] helps them [result], unlike [current alternative].**

## Local example

Arun turned the best problems into idea statements:

- **ShopAssist:** For shop owners in Kuttiady and Vatakara who lose evening WhatsApp enquiries, a one-day WhatsApp Business and Google profile setup helps them answer in minutes with prices and photos, unlike a family member replying late at night.
- **Nisha's Oven:** For parents near Kuttiady who want home-made birthday cakes without artificial colours, a home bakery with WhatsApp ordering delivers within 5 km, unlike a trip to Vatakara.

A rough size check for Nisha: about 3,000 households in her delivery area (her own estimate from ward lists), 2 cakes per household per year, and perhaps 1 in 5 of those cakes bought from a home baker. That gives 3,000 × 2 × 0.2 = 1,200 cakes a year. At ₹750 a cake, the reachable market is about ₹9 lakh a year. She needs only a small share, say 4 cakes a week, for a useful side income. The inputs are guesses, but they show the idea is worth testing.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Google Trends](https://trends.google.com/trends/) | Set the region to Kerala and compare 3 search terms linked to your problems over the past 5 years | 20 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 5](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/5-introduction) | Sections 5.2 Researching Potential Business Opportunities and 5.3 Competitive Analysis | 45 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [Kerala: One Local Body One Product (OLOP)](https://industry.kerala.gov.in/index.php/schemes-mainmenu/one-local-body-one-product-olop) | Read what the scheme supports (check current rules) | 10 min | verified 2026-10-24; check current rules |

## Action task

1. List 10 things people in your area travel out of town to buy or get done. Ask two older relatives to add to the list.
2. Ask three shopkeepers: "What do customers ask for that you don't sell?" Write down their answers word for word.
3. In Google Trends (region: Kerala), compare search interest for terms linked to your top problems. Note which ones are growing or seasonal.
4. Write 10 idea statements in the Ideas tab using the template below. Cover at least two of the four paths.
5. For your top three ideas, do a bottom-up size check and list five alternatives each.

**Proof to record:** Your 10 idea statements, the three shopkeepers' answers, and size checks with alternatives for your top three ideas.

## Template: idea statement and size check

```
IDEA STATEMENT
For [customer] ____________ who [problem] ____________,
[offer] ____________ helps them [result] ____________,
unlike [current alternative] ____________.

QUICK SIZE CHECK
Customers I can reach: ____
Purchases per customer per year: ____
Price (₹): ____
Market per year = customers x purchases x price = ₹ ____
Sales a week I need for my goal: ____

ALTERNATIVES (at least 5)
1. Do nothing
2. Do it themselves
3. ____
4. ____
5. ____
```

## Common mistakes

- **Using huge numbers.** "India is a big market" tells you nothing. Count the customers you could reach this month.
- **Ignoring seasons.** A cake business in Christmas week and in the monsoon are two different businesses. Plan for the slow months too.
- **Opening the sixth copy.** If your town already has five mobile shops, a sixth must be clearly different. Count competitors before you choose.
- **Forgetting that "do nothing" competes.** Many customers simply live with a problem. Your offer must be clearly better than doing nothing.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does Google Trends show?
    - A) The exact number of searches
    - B) Relative search interest over time and by region
    - C) Your competitors' sales
    - D) How many customers you will get
2. You can reach 500 shops, each might buy 1 setup a year, at ₹1,500. What is the bottom-up market per year?
    - A) ₹75,000
    - B) ₹7.5 lakh
    - C) ₹75 lakh
    - D) ₹1,500
3. Which is the best idea statement?
    - A) "A great bakery"
    - B) "For parents near Kuttiady who want home-made birthday cakes without artificial colours, a home bakery with WhatsApp ordering delivers within 5 km, unlike a trip to Vatakara"
    - C) "Cakes for everyone"
    - D) "The best cakes in Kerala"
4. Why list "do nothing" as an alternative?
    - A) To fill the list
    - B) Many customers will simply live with the problem, so your offer has to beat that
    - C) It is a legal requirement
    - D) Investors ask for it

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Google Trends practice, OpenStax 5.2 and 5.3, and the OLOP page (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
- **Action:** map opportunities, ask three shopkeepers, write 10 idea statements and size your top three. It is done when your proof is saved: your 10 idea statements, the three shopkeepers' answers, and size checks with alternatives for your top three ideas.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Use it to compare terms and spot seasons, not to count customers.
2. **B.** 500 × 1 × ₹1,500 = ₹7,50,000.
3. **B.** It names the customer, the problem, the offer, the result and the alternative.
4. **B.** Inaction is the most common competitor for a new small business.

sections.title: ENT-M02-L03: Score your ideas and choose one to test
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Score your ideas with a weighted scorecard, choose one idea and two backups, and write a test hypothesis with a kill signal. **Time:** about 4 hours (1.5 hours study, 2.5 hours action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

You now have more ideas than time. Scoring them makes your choice honest, and lets you explain it to someone else.

### Kill criteria come first

Before scoring, cross out any idea that:

- is illegal, unsafe or misleading
- needs more money than your risk limit before the first sale
- needs a licence you can't get, such as one for selling medicines
- needs full-time hours you don't have

### The weighted scorecard

Score each remaining idea from 1 to 5 on each row, multiply by the weight and add up. The highest possible total is 90.

| Criterion | Weight | Ask yourself |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem pain | 3 | How much does the problem hurt, in money, time or stress? |
| Willingness to pay | 3 | Do people already pay for a workaround? |
| Customer access | 2 | Can I reach 20 of these customers this month? |
| Fit with my path and skills | 2 | Can I deliver it now, or learn how in 4 weeks? |
| Low start cost | 2 | Can I test it within my risk limit? |
| Time to first rupee | 2 | Could someone pay me within 30 days? |
| Simple rules | 1 | Can I start without hard-to-get licences? |
| Different from others | 1 | Is it clearly different from what people use now? |
| Interest | 1 | Will I still care about it in six months? |
| Long-term potential | 1 | Could it grow into a real income? |

Pain and willingness to pay carry the most weight because a business without them can't survive, however clever it is.

### Sanity questions

Y Combinator's talk on evaluating ideas asks questions like these. Answer them honestly for your top three:

1. Are you the right person for this idea (founder–market fit)?
2. How big could the market be, and is it growing?
3. How urgent is the problem? Will people pay to fix it now?
4. Who else solves it, and why would people choose you?
5. Do you want this yourself, or personally know people who do?

### Write a test hypothesis

A hypothesis turns your choice into something you can prove wrong:

**I believe [customer] will pay [₹ amount] for [offer] because [problem]. I'll know I'm wrong if [kill signal] by [date].**

The kill signal is the result that tells you to stop or change course, for example "fewer than 3 of 15 shop owners agree to a paid trial by the end of week 10".

Scores are a starting bet, not the truth. The next two modules exist to test them with real people.

## Local example

Arun scored four ideas (each cell shows score × weight):

| Criterion (weight) | ShopAssist | PSC Sprint | Bill-pay help for elders | Home bakery |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pain (3) | 4 = 12 | 3 = 9 | 4 = 12 | 3 = 9 |
| Pay (3) | 4 = 12 | 3 = 9 | 2 = 6 | 4 = 12 |
| Access (2) | 5 = 10 | 4 = 8 | 3 = 6 | 3 = 6 |
| Fit (2) | 4 = 8 | 4 = 8 | 3 = 6 | 1 = 2 |
| Start cost (2) | 5 = 10 | 5 = 10 | 5 = 10 | 3 = 6 |
| First ₹ (2) | 5 = 10 | 3 = 6 | 3 = 6 | 4 = 8 |
| Rules (1) | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| Different (1) | 3 | 3 | 4 | 2 |
| Interest (1) | 4 | 4 | 3 | 1 |
| Potential (1) | 4 | 3 | 2 | 3 |
| **Total (of 90)** | **78** | **64** | **58** | **51** |

ShopAssist wins for Arun. His hypothesis: "I believe textile and mobile shop owners in Kuttiady and Vatakara will pay ₹1,500 for a one-day WhatsApp Business and Google profile setup, because they lose evening enquiries. I'll know I'm wrong if fewer than 3 of 15 owners agree to a paid setup by the end of week 10." PSC Sprint and the bill-pay help are his backups. Nisha, a keen baker with no interest in shop software, or Fathima, who ranked on a PSC list last year, would score the same ideas very differently, and that is the point.

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [YC: "How to Get and Evaluate Startup Ideas" (Jared Friedman)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Th8JoIan4dg) | Watch the whole talk; pause at the list of questions for evaluating an idea and write your answers | about 25 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 4](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/4-introduction) | Section 4.3 Developing Ideas, Innovations, and Inventions | 30 min | verified 2026-10-24 |
| [OpenStax Entrepreneurship, Chapter 11](https://openstax.org/books/entrepreneurship/pages/11-introduction) | Section 11.3 Conducting a Feasibility Analysis | 30 min | verified 2026-10-24 |

## Action task

1. Cross out every idea that fails a kill criterion.
2. Score the rest with the scorecard below. In the "Weighted total" row, type =SUMPRODUCT($B3:$B12,C3:C12) in column C and copy it across. Score one row at a time across all ideas; it is harder to favour your pet idea that way.
3. Ask two people who know you to score only "fit" and "interest" for your top five. If they disagree strongly and you can't explain why, change your score.
4. For your top idea, have three 5-minute chats with people who have the problem. Ask: "When did this last happen? What did you do?" Don't pitch. If none of the three recognise the problem, look again at your second idea.
5. Write your test hypothesis with a kill signal and a date, and name your two backups.

**Proof to record:** Your completed scorecard, notes from the three quick chats and your written hypothesis.

## Template: weighted scorecard (paste into the Ideas tab)

```csv
Criterion,Weight,Idea 1,Idea 2,Idea 3,Idea 4,Idea 5
Idea name,,,,,,
Problem pain,3,,,,,
Willingness to pay,3,,,,,
Customer access,2,,,,,
Fit with my skills,2,,,,,
Low start cost,2,,,,,
Time to first rupee,2,,,,,
Simple rules,1,,,,,
Different from others,1,,,,,
Interest,1,,,,,
Long-term potential,1,,,,,
Weighted total,,,,,,
```

## Template: test hypothesis

```
TEST HYPOTHESIS
I believe [customer] ____________
will pay [₹] ____ for [offer] ____________
because [problem] ____________.
I'll know I'm wrong if [kill signal] ____________
by [date] ____________.

Backup 1: ____________
Backup 2: ____________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Scoring your favourite idea high everywhere.** Score one row across all ideas at a time, and get a second opinion on fit and interest.
- **Ignoring access.** A great idea for customers you can't reach is a poor first idea. Access is what makes testing fast.
- **Treating the scores as truth.** They are guesses until customers confirm them. Modules 3 and 4 test them.
- **A hypothesis with no kill signal.** Without a number and a date, you will keep going on hope alone.

## Quiz

Answer without looking back. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Why multiply each score by a weight?
    - A) To make the numbers bigger
    - B) Because some criteria, like pain and willingness to pay, matter more than others
    - C) Banks require it
    - D) To confuse competitors
2. Which idea should be crossed out before scoring?
    - A) One that needs ₹50,000 before any sale when your risk limit is ₹5,000
    - B) One with little competition
    - C) One you love
    - D) One in your own town
3. Which is a good kill signal?
    - A) "If people don't like it"
    - B) "If fewer than 3 of 15 owners agree to a paid setup by the end of week 10"
    - C) "If I get bored"
    - D) "If it doesn't go viral"
4. Your top idea scores 78, but none of three people with the problem recognise it. What next?
    - A) Ignore them and build it
    - B) Look again at your second idea, or rewrite the problem and test again
    - C) Raise the price
    - D) Register a company

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** the YC talk on evaluating ideas, OpenStax 4.3 and 11.3 (about 1.5 hours)
- **Action:** score your ideas, have three quick chats about the top one and write your hypothesis. It is done when your proof is saved: your completed scorecard, notes from the three quick chats and your written hypothesis.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again.

## Answers

1. **B.** Weights make the criteria that decide survival count for more.
2. **A.** It breaks a kill criterion: it needs more money than you can afford to lose.
3. **B.** It has a number, a group of people and a date, so you can't argue with it later.
4. **B.** Real people outrank your scores. Adjust before you spend more time.
